stories.topic: The Fan Who Wanted Them to Plan India's Economy
stories.summary: A fan sent Amit a gushing email that ended with two lines he found deeply disturbing: 'you guys are so smart, I wish you were running the country. You should plan our economy.' Amit replied with three objections. First, you can't run a country like a YouTube show, a play on their episode 'Don't Run a Country Like a Company'. Second, power corrupts, and whatever humility the two of them have comes from setbacks, not success. Third, the word 'plan' itself: you can plan your day or a shoot schedule, but planning a nation is the hubris Hayek called the fatal conceit.
stories.insight: Being good at one thing does not qualify you to steer a society. The flattering wish to put 'smart people on top' is the same top-down instinct that produces industrial policy.
stories.quote: You can't run a country like a YouTube show. We are good at running this YouTube show.

stories.topic: A Callow 35-Year-Old Meets the Finance Ministry
stories.summary: As a young economist, Ajay assumed the policy world was full of stupid mistakes he could easily improve on. At 35 he joined the Ministry of Finance, hired by Yashwant Sinha, whom he admires enormously and calls one of the great people of the country. He worked intensively with Sinha, and within days he realised that being finance minister is extremely hard. There were no obvious mistakes and no low-hanging fruit.
stories.insight: From outside, government looks like a list of easy fixes. From inside, the hard problems are hard for real reasons. That humility is the starting point for the whole case against planners who think they know best.
stories.quote: very hard to be a finance minister and there are no obvious mistakes. It's like there are no low hanging fruit

stories.summary: At a Ministry of Finance meeting run by Ashok Lahiri, then chief economic advisor, the routine business included the Ministry of Commerce setting an export target for India. Ajay, the junior-most person in the room, asked what the Ministry of Commerce, or any of them, had to do with what India exports. Individual firms make export decisions, and the state's job is only to create enabling conditions. Even the word 'target' is semi-offensive, because missing it triggers urgent mid-year meetings about 'policy measures to boost exports'.
stories.insight: The abstraction 'India' hides who actually acts. Firms export, not the state. Treating the nation as one agent with targets is the root of the control mindset behind industrial policy.
stories.quote: And the Indian state has essentially nothing to do with the exporting decisions or the exporting success of individual firms.

stories.topic: Nanotech and Poultry: The RBI's Chosen Industries
stories.summary: The RBI has long imposed capital controls on foreign borrowing, and Ajay says he has never seen an economic reason for them. One day a rule restricted external commercial borrowing to just nine industries, so the chosen ones would get access to cheaper foreign credit and the rest would not. Ajay, 'bloody minded and masochistic' enough to actually read such documents, found that the chosen industries included nanotechnology and poultry farms.
stories.insight: This is what 'picking winners' looks like in practice: an arbitrary list that hands some sectors a privilege while denying it to others, and nobody could defend the choices on economic grounds.
stories.quote: Chicken needs cheap credit. So we will give exclusive access to external commercial borrowing to poultry farms.

stories.topic: UPI by Decree, GPS by Choice
stories.summary: Their friend Suyash observed that the government picked UPI as the technology and then used income tax law to back it: income tax inspectors can fine any shop that does not accept UPI. Amit called this a TIL and argued that even though UPI is outstanding technology, every shopkeeper should be free to choose how to accept payment. Ajay contrasted it with the US. He recalls that around 1993 Bill Clinton signed off on releasing high-resolution GPS data to the whole world. People rushed to adopt it, yet the government never mandated it. Phone makers themselves aspired to put GPS in every phone.
stories.insight: A good technology wins adoption without force. Reaching for coercion first is a distinctly Indian habit, and it shuts down the competition through which better options emerge.
stories.quote: Okay, so it is a very Indian malaise, the low trigger point for the use of coercive power, and we should watch out for it.

stories.summary: Amit grew up in a privileged household, with a father in the civil service. Even so, in the 1980s you waited seven or eight years for a telephone from the MTNL monopoly. Air fares were about 8,000 rupees, roughly what they cost now but a huge sum then, so even an officer's family rarely flew. He still remembers the excitement of his first flight. After 1991, when these sectors opened up, competitors flooded in and prices fell. MTNL and BSNL were never shut down; they simply became irrelevant. Many TV channels arrived too, and nobody had to watch Doordarshan anymore. He retells this often because about 70% of Indians were born after liberalisation.
stories.insight: The cost of a state monopoly is easy to forget once it is gone. The same test applies to every sector that is still closed: what would competition do there?
stories.quote: it's not that they were shut down, it's just that they became completely irrelevant.

stories.summary: Air India began as a private company owned by the Tatas. The government expropriated it and made it a monopoly. When the airline industry was later opened to competition, Air India turned into a zombie firm that, at its peak, Ajay believes was bleeding about 35,000 crore rupees a year in taxpayer subsidy. The BJP government eventually privatised it back to the Tatas, which Ajay calls a great achievement. He asks what would have happened if it had never been nationalised, and why Lufthansa doesn't fly Bombay–Delhi.
stories.insight: Privatisation recovers only part of the loss. The real cost is the decades of competition, service and growth that never happened.
stories.quote: But it just makes you wonder, what if Air India had never been nationalized in the first place? What if it had been a private firm all through?

stories.topic: SEEPZ: The Radio Plan That Birthed Diamonds and Software
stories.summary: In the 1970s, bureaucrats saw East Asia exporting radios and electronic parts and asked why India couldn't do the same. They diagnosed the problem as customs duty: paying 150% on imported transistors made Indian-made radios impossible to export. So in the boondocks of North Bombay they walled off land as the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ). Every truck through its gate was inspected. Components came in from the airport under guard, Ajay imagines with a shotgun rider, so nothing leaked into the Indian market, and finished goods went straight back out to planes. Given this pocket of freedom to import and export, entrepreneurs discovered things nobody planned. One was polishing rough diamonds brought from South Africa and Antwerp; India today polishes about 55% of the world's diamonds by number. The other was importing computers so Indian programmers could build and export software, making SEEPZ one of the early sites of the Indian software industry.
stories.insight: Ajay calls it one of the greatest industrial-policy successes in history, but it worked because it added freedom, not because anyone picked the right industry. The two big winners were ones no planner foresaw.
stories.quote: you can't predict, you can't control, but adding freedom is always a good thing. Increasing freedom is always a good thing.

recommendations.item: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Amit invoked 'our hero' Hayek while explaining why he dislikes the word 'plan' applied to a country.
recommendations.reason: Hayek's phrase names the core error of the whole episode: a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top.

recommendations.context: Ajay was a guest on Rahul's chat show and spoke for about an hour on industrial policy.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a lovely chat and the companion to this episode's subject.

recommendations.reason: It explains why business intuitions don't carry over to public policy, which is the trap behind many calls for industrial policy.

recommendations.reason: Amit says he is very proud of producing them because Ajay shared tremendous insights through all of them.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Raised while contrasting India's rent-seeking business mentality with firms that compete globally.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended during the discussion of the state forcing shops to accept UPI; Ajay cited it again in the coercion chapter.
recommendations.reason: It examines 'allegedly' public digital infrastructure and why mandated state monopolies like UPI crowd out competing payment systems.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21) and The Journey of Indian Finance (Episode 71), Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's answer to the objection that India's financial system is too weak, so the government must hand out money itself.
recommendations.reason: A lot is known about fixing Indian finance, so fix the root cause instead of replacing finance with government. He asks listeners to send these episodes to friends in public policy.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended explicitly after his explanation of Milton Friedman's spending matrix.
recommendations.reason: Don't think of the state as a benevolent beast. It is individuals responding to incentives, which explains who captures subsidy decisions and why.

recommendations.item: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Rauch
recommendations.context: Cited while discussing rent-seeking and special interests.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great book on how special interests took over the American system. It was written in the 1990s and is still true today, a reminder that rent-seeking isn't only an Indian problem.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's answer to 'how hard is it to fix the indirect tax system instead of doing PLI?'
recommendations.reason: It sets out the public policy process: gather data, do research, hold public debate, write committee reports and draft laws. Not six weeks, maybe six months, surely six years.

recommendations.item: The Power of Moore's Laws (Episode 87, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while arguing that productivity lives in know-how, not machines.
recommendations.reason: It covers Wright's Law, the learning-by-doing process inside better firms.

recommendations.item: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's setup for the 'but look at China' question; Ajay summarised its essence in his answer.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an excellent episode. It shows that Chinese state control and industrial policy caused deep problems behind the cherry-picked EV and solar successes.

recommendations.item: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited in the final chapter on what the state should do instead.
recommendations.reason: It describes an industry-neutral, contracting-out approach to R&D, with grants to universities and private firms, as opposed to bureaucrats picking sectors.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited in the 'enable winners' chapter.
recommendations.reason: Bankruptcy is a healthy, normal part of life. Firms must be able to fail and people must be able to land on their feet.

recommendations.context: Cited while arguing for more immigration into India.
recommendations.reason: It makes the point that a truly great firm recruits from all over the world, which is why India's visa rules need to change.

recommendations.creator: Akhsay Jaitley and Ajay Shah

recommendations.reason: An example of working through the price system instead of the state picking favoured technologies.

core_ideas.concept: The Fatal Conceit: Nations Can't Be Planned
core_ideas.explanation: You can plan your own day, but a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top. Top-down thinking leads to ruin again and again, however enlightened the planners believe their approach is. Amit holds that industrial policy should not be done better; it should not be done at all.
core_ideas.quote: Planning a country is just a conception of great hubris. Our hero Friedrich Hayek called it the fatal conceit. It simply cannot be done. A nation is too complex.

core_ideas.concept: Industrial Policy Means Picking Winners, Using Four Levers
core_ideas.explanation: When the government decides which industry, technology, firm or location is good or bad, that is industrial policy. It works through four levers: subsidies (public money, tax breaks), coercive power (for example, fining shops that don't take UPI), ethno-nationalism (favour Indian firms, keep foreigners out), and outright government monopolies. In the first, the state plays venture capitalist; in the last, it plays entrepreneur.
core_ideas.quote: All these kinds of allocative decisions about how the economy works. When these are placed in the hands of the government, it's called industrial policy.

core_ideas.concept: Clusters Emerge, They Can't Be Willed
core_ideas.explanation: Silicon Valley, Tirupur's garments and Gujarat's chemicals grew organically. Skills, vendors and labour markets accumulated and created network effects. Governments see this and try to declare clusters, and the decisions get contaminated by 'equity' (every state deserves one, so a drug cluster in Himachal Pradesh) or by a powerful politician's constituency.
core_ideas.quote: So it is true that clusters develop, clusters matter, clusters shape productivity. It is not true that you can will these into existence.

core_ideas.concept: Economic Development Is a Story of Firms
core_ideas.explanation: By simple arithmetic, GDP is the sum of the value added by all firms. A rich country is full of high-productivity firms and a poor one is full of low-productivity firms. People are the same everywhere; Sundar Pichai and Satya Nadella are Indians. The difference lies in the incentives created by the firms' operating environment.
core_ideas.quote: And so the story of economic development is centrally a story of firms.

core_ideas.concept: Coercion Has No Budget Constraint
core_ideas.explanation: Spending is limited by taxes, deficits and competing claims, because the budget has to add up. Coercive power has no such limit, so the state can keep adding restrictions every day at no budget cost. That is why coercion spreads so easily through industrial policy.
core_ideas.quote: There's no budget constraint of coercive power. Every day the Indian state shackles you some more.

core_ideas.concept: Finance Works Through Failure
core_ideas.explanation: If an industry has good prospects, investors will fund it with equity or debt, because looking for the next good opportunity is what finance does all day. The system works by placing many bets on long shots, most of which fail. A government instead backs one national champion through thick and thin. If the financial system is weak, the fix is to repair it and let foreign financial firms in, not to replace it with the state.
core_ideas.quote: Finance works through failure. Okay, it is just magical. The financial system through dozens and dozens and dozens of long shots, and some of them work. Most of them fail. That's the glory of finance.

core_ideas.concept: The Marginal Cost of Public Funds Is About Three
core_ideas.explanation: Public money is taken from people by force. People reorganise their lives and firms to avoid tax, which lowers productivity, and the economy also bears the overhead of compliance, lawyers and enforcement. Each rupee the government spends therefore costs the economy about three. Only public goods and real market failures, such as defence, foreign policy or a vaccination campaign, return enough to justify that. Subsidising poultry or textiles does not.
core_ideas.quote: Public money is coerced out of the people. Okay? Taxation has blood on it.

core_ideas.concept: Intervention Redistributes From the Poor to the Rich
core_ideas.explanation: Socialists believe interventions move wealth from rich to poor. Amit argues the reverse happens: costs are spread thinly and invisibly across everyone, while the benefits go to concentrated interests. The poor pay most, often by staying poor longer than they otherwise would.
core_ideas.quote: I often say that every intervention in free markets amounts to a redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.concept: Milton Friedman's Spending Matrix
core_ideas.explanation: Spending your own money on yourself, you economise and seek value. Your money on others: you economise but care less about value. Others' money on yourself: you seek value but don't economise. Government spends other people's money on other people, so it does neither.
core_ideas.quote: What the government does is that it spends somebody else's money on somebody else. And therefore the incentives drive you towards neither economizing nor towards seeking value. It is the worst way to spend money.

core_ideas.concept: Public Choice and the Power Paradox
core_ideas.explanation: Officials are not selfless, all-knowing welfare maximisers; they are ordinary people pursuing their own careers and goals. Investors have skin in the game and are judged on results, so they pay for information and research. Bureaucrats have little incentive to learn, and everyone who visits them flatters them ('Sir, you are so great... just one small thing, your subsidy scheme should work well for my industry'). Power cuts them off from honest information, which leads to more confidence, more control and even worse information. Ajay calls this the socialist trap.
core_ideas.quote: Once the government amasses power, they get cut off from knowledge.

core_ideas.concept: A Country Is Not a Company: The Double Error
core_ideas.explanation: Engineers and businesspeople who are convinced about, say, lithium-ion batteries leap to wanting state power behind them. Government is a different arena, with its own rules: political economy, public administration, checks and balances, rule of law. Their reasoning also contains two errors: assuming they know what's right for the world, and assuming they'd be the joint secretary making the call.
core_ideas.quote: And second, I'm the guy that will be the joint secretary. Bracket, you won't. Okay. Both stages of this reasoning are wrong.

core_ideas.concept: The Rent-Seeking Mentality of a Protected Economy
core_ideas.explanation: For decades India had a protected economy run by a powerful state. Firms got ahead by working the state rather than by serving customers better than global rivals, and that habit has become a mindset. An American entrepreneur asks how to create enough value to get rich; too often an Indian one asks how to influence a joint secretary to beat local competitors.
core_ideas.quote: The way to therefore get ahead in India has always been that you suck up to the state, you use the levers of the state, and either you become a crony directly or you try to influence it.

core_ideas.concept: PLI Patches Tax Mistakes Deal by Deal
core_ideas.explanation: The average Indian non-financial firm makes about 6% profit after tax on sales, so a 1–3% indirect-tax error can swing the return on equity by 50–100%. Ajay credits Ila Patnaik with teaching him this. Good countries refund indirect taxes on exports because you don't tax foreigners. India doesn't, so Apple is right to demand compensation, and PLI provides it. But PLI only reaches giants that can afford roughly a $10 million policy operation in Delhi to negotiate and actually get paid. Fixing the tax system at the root would attract the thousands of firms that won't bother.
core_ideas.quote: PLI is a reversal of inappropriate taxation. Okay. A simple dharma of public finance is you don't tax non-residents.

core_ideas.concept: Real Disabilities vs. Whining (the Negative Disability)
core_ideas.explanation: Tax mistakes are genuine disabilities created by the state and should be fixed. Expensive transport, unreliable electricity and unskilled workers are ordinary features of producing anywhere, and no government should compensate firms for them. India's very low wages are a huge advantage in the firm's pocket. Ajay credits Rahul Ahluwalia with the point that the real surprise is how little India exports, given labour costs that low.
core_ideas.quote: you're operating in India, some of the lowest wages in the world, you've got a huge sort of negative disability in your pocket.

core_ideas.concept: Engineer's Technology vs. Economist's Technology
core_ideas.explanation: States force particular technologies on the economy believing productivity lives in the machine. It mostly lives in tacit knowledge, process and management, which are learned by doing (Wright's Law). Giving an army great tanks doesn't make it world-class. Know-how spreads through people, such as Hindustan Lever alumni who carried Unilever's knowledge into new consumer goods companies. Ajay also argues that multiple rival standards competing for supremacy are healthy.
core_ideas.quote: To an engineer, a technology is a machine. Okay, to an economist, technology is everything about technique.

core_ideas.concept: Foreign Firms Are India's Best Teachers
core_ideas.explanation: The global state of the art lives inside foreign firms, so their presence spreads productivity across India. 'Indian firm' is a slippery idea anyway: ICICI Bank is 90% foreign-owned and Microsoft has an Indian CEO. Apple's presence could push Indian vendors from hundred-micron to one-micron tolerances, much as Texas Instruments helped seed Indian IT.
core_ideas.quote: If anything you want it upside down. You want more foreign firms here, because foreign firms command that highest knowledge.

core_ideas.concept: The Two Unseen Effects of Protectionism
core_ideas.explanation: Suppose a tariff protects Indian firm A from a better Italian firm X. The visible effect is that A prospers. The first unseen effect is that consumers lose lower prices or better value, which is a dispersed transfer to a concentrated beneficiary. The second is that A no longer has to match the global best, so it stays stuck in a low-productivity equilibrium.
core_ideas.quote: So you're not even helping the Indian company. You're hurting the consumer and you're hurting the Indian company.

core_ideas.concept: Wall Off National Security; GDP Is the Real Defence
core_ideas.explanation: The army has real reasons to avoid Chinese gear that may contain backdoors, given the border tensions at Doklam and Galwan. It should solve that for itself, through trusted supply chains and partnerships with like-minded actors. Ajay cites Europe working on drones without Chinese backdoors and Ukraine, now one of the world's largest drone producers, avoiding Chinese parts. That is no reason to be anti-foreign across the whole economy. Strategic strength comes from growth: Russia's GDP is Italy-sized, which is why Europe can absorb the threat.
core_ideas.quote: you have to wall off the military problem from the economy problem. And in fact, the greatest path to military strength and successful foreign policy lies in eight percent GDP growth.

core_ideas.concept: The China Question: Don't Cherry-Pick
core_ideas.explanation: Chinese EVs and solar panels are real successes, but they are picked out from a long list of failures. Taken as a whole, Chinese state control and industrial policy produced about 1.5 apartments per household, a shrinking population and lost dynamism under Xi Jinping. China's per capita GDP remains far below that of advanced economies.
core_ideas.quote: all successful advanced economies look alike. All unhappy, poor countries are unhappy in their own way.

core_ideas.concept: Enable Winners, Don't Pick Them
core_ideas.explanation: Unknown geniuses are hidden in the private sector, and the state's job is to create conditions in which some of them win. Ajay's list: industry-neutral R&D contracts and grants that push the limits of knowledge, whose spillovers nobody can predict; fierce competition from startup to bankruptcy, so firms keep striving; deep internationalisation with free imports and exports, Indian multinationals and unrestricted foreign firms; and open immigration of talent. Amit adds a caution: limit the state to rule of law, because most monopolies exist only with the state's collusion.
core_ideas.quote: The job of government is to create conditions where winning happens, where some great firms emerge with really high productivities.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's version of the classic $500-bill joke. A Bengali economist who believes in rational markets walks past a 500-rupee note, reasoning that if it were real someone would have picked it up already. Then a Gujarati YouTuber ('hint hint, wink wink') spots it and says not 'money' but 'content', and sets up his selfie stick to film himself discovering it. Meanwhile Amit Varma walks up from behind and pockets it. 'The story doesn't end well for either of our two protagonists.'

Ajay's twist: the bill is superglued to the ground, and a prank crew from a 'whiskey triceps' show is filming people trying to pick it up. Amit insists it must alliterate like Beer Biceps and offers 'tequila triceps', 'hamburger hamstrings' and 'brandy balls'.
After Ajay says he publicly declared his official occupation as YouTuber, Amit: 'So you are henceforth not an economist. You're a card carrying YouTuber.'

On the RBI letting poultry farms borrow abroad: 'Amit, you're not eating enough chicken. Chicken needs cheap credit.' Amit's comeback: 'Picking chickens in nanotechnology and resulting in really tiny chickens... we have nano chickens.'

Ajay claims YouTube says most viewers are engineers. Amit: 'Wait a minute, what analytics are you examining? This is nowhere in the analytics.' Ajay: 'Young males and almost all young males in India are engineers.' Amit: 'No, many creative women watch our show, I mean partly mainly because of me.' After Ajay's rant against engineers jumping to industrial policy, Amit adds: 'Gentle readers, Ajay Shah is an engineer.'
Ajay's tribute to the show's own camera crew: 'If any idiot had a Sony Alpha DSLR, they do not become Nomsita.'

Amit on Ajay's coinage 'negative disability': 'At some point someday, Ajay Shah, people are gonna come and hit on you and they'll say things like Ajay, you have so many negative disabilities.' Ajay can't find a snappy reply, and Amit tells him to bring one next episode.

Amit's riddle: a dear leader appoints a secretary for each system of organs, a digestion secretary for the stomach and a respiration secretary for the lungs. What do you call the one in charge of his elbows, knees and ankles? Ajay gets it (the joint secretary, the bureaucratic rank mocked all episode), and Amit says: 'Well done. I'm so proud of you.'
After Ajay calls Russia 'an Italy-sized GDP', Amit says many, many Italian viewers are at this point deeply disappointed.
Amit on how fast technology moves: 'Today's cutting edge is passe by midnight and obsolete by noon tomorrow.'
Ajay's ideal industry-neutral research agenda includes landing a craft on Venus ('a nonsensical objective') and grants on how to double the size of an egg: 'We want Wright's law of eggs.'
Amit's SEEPZ pun: the Allman Brothers Band came to perform there, everyone was let in, but one member was examined. Who? Derek Trucks, 'because we were examining all the trucks.'

The recommendations heist. Amit complains that every episode he proposes a recommendations chapter, the crew 'break their silence and say yes, yes, yes,' and Ajay says 'forget it, next time.' Then Ajay answers Amit's Duane Allman quiz with 'Layla' and declares it 'my recommendation for today'. Amit: 'You cannot fucking do this. I had already named the song. This was gonna be my recommendation.' Ajay: 'I promise next episode, I will have five recommendations.'
Friedrich Hayek's 'fatal conceit': Amit's name for the hubris of planning a nation, and the intellectual backbone of the episode.
The '$500 bill lying on the ground', the economists' parable about efficient markets. It titles the intro, and Ajay uses it for his lesson that real policy has no obvious easy wins.
Amit quotes the famous maxim 'Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely' and adds that, more than anything, it corrupts character.
Oliver Cromwell, cited by Ajay against governments sure of their technology bets: 'in the bowels of Christ, consider it possible you may be mistaken.'
Milton Friedman's matrix of spending your own or someone else's money on yourself or on others, which Amit uses to show why government spending is the worst kind.
Wright's Law, the learning-by-doing process inside better firms, which Ajay cites to argue that productivity lives in know-how rather than machines.
Ajay's twist on the opening line of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina: 'All successful advanced economies look alike. All unhappy, poor countries are unhappy in their own way.'
Pai of the Takshashila Institution, whom Amit quotes as often saying the best foreign policy is a rising GDP.

The seen and the unseen: Amit applies the framing his podcast is named after to tariffs. The seen effect is the protected firm prospering; the unseen effects are consumers paying more and the firm never improving.
